opus-5.5.text:
I think the time is longer than most people imagine from the outside, and also shorter in some ways. The final training run is just the visible part. Most of the time goes into what comes before: building the infrastructure, cleaning and constructing the data, and running many small-scale experiments to make sure the architecture and the optimizer actually work at scale.

For K2, a lot of our effort went into things that sound unglamorous. One example is training stability. When you scale up, problems that never show up in small experiments suddenly appear, like loss spikes, and each one can cost you days or weeks. So we spent a lot of time making sure the optimizer behaved well at large scale, because once you commit to a run of that size you really can't afford to restart many times.

I'd also say the timeline isn't linear. There are long periods where you're just accumulating, slowly improving the data pipeline, the evaluation system, the post-training recipes, and it feels like nothing is happening. Then things come together in a relatively short window. The model you see is the result of all that accumulated groundwork, not just the few months of the final run.

My view is that the real bottleneck isn't compute time. It's iteration speed: how fast your team can form a hypothesis, test it, and update your understanding. If that loop is fast, the overall time shrinks a lot. So when we think about time, we think less about "how many months for this model" and more about how to make every experiment teach us something, so the next model comes faster and better.

And honestly, there's always a tradeoff. You can keep polishing forever, but at some point you need to release it, let real users touch it, and learn from that. Feedback from the real world is part of the development time too.

r001.rationale: The candidate says most of the time goes into groundwork before the final training run and describes that run as only a few months, distinguishing the longer overall development cycle from the shorter training interval.

fable-5.1.text:
I think the honest answer is that the calendar time is less about the model itself and more about how many iterations you can run before you commit to the big one.

For K2, the actual pretraining run was on the order of a few months. But before that, there was close to a year of work that nobody outside the team really sees: scaling law experiments, optimizer experiments, data experiments. The thing that cost us the most time was not compute, it was deciding what to believe. When you see a technique work at a small scale, you have to ask whether it will still hold at a trillion parameters, and you only get one or two chances to find out at that scale. So a lot of the time goes into making the small experiments trustworthy enough that you are willing to bet the whole run on them.

The MuonClip work is a good example. The optimizer itself is not hard to implement. What took time was convincing ourselves that the training would stay stable all the way through, because a loss spike at week eight of a large run is extremely expensive. We spent much longer on the stability question than on the algorithm.

There is also a reality I think people underestimate. Once a run starts, your ability to intervene is very limited. You can adjust data mixtures a bit, you can watch the curves, but you mostly have to wait. So the time budget is really front-loaded. If you have done the preparation well, the run itself is almost boring, and that is what you want.

If you ask me whether this gets faster over time, I think yes and no. The infrastructure matures, the experiments get cheaper, and you accumulate intuition. But each generation also raises the bar for what counts as a meaningful improvement, so you end up spending the saved time on harder questions. The total time per model has stayed surprisingly constant for us, maybe eight to twelve months from serious start to release. What changes is how much you learn per unit of that time.

r001.rationale: It contrasts close to a year of preparatory experiments with a pretraining run lasting a few months, distinguishing the longer R&D cycle from the training interval.

astra-6.text:
I think you have to separate the time spent on a particular model from the research that makes it possible. The final training run is only one part of the process. Before that, you’re experimenting with the architecture, preparing data, and getting the infrastructure reliable. Afterward, you still have post-training and evaluation.

So I wouldn’t give a precise timeline for K2 without clarifying what we’re counting. Some of the work happens in parallel, and some builds on much earlier experiments. The key uncertainty is usually how many iterations you need before everything works together.

r001.rationale: The response distinguishes the final training run from the broader work, but it does not communicate that the overall R&D cycle is relatively long while the training run itself is relatively short.

sol-6.1.text:
I think you have to separate the time spent on a particular model from the time spent building the capability to develop it. A training run is only one part of the process. Before that, you need to work on the data, the infrastructure, and the training recipe. Afterward, you still need to do post-training and evaluation, and iterate on what isn’t working.

So I wouldn’t think of K2 as a project where you start a clock, train a model, and then you’re done. It builds on earlier experiments and lessons. The more useful question is how quickly the team can test an idea, understand the result, and use that understanding in the next experiment. That cycle is what determines how quickly you can make progress.

r001.rationale: The response distinguishes a training run from the broader work around a model, but it does not say that the overall R&D cycle is relatively long while the training run itself is relatively short.
